name: Hook Mate
summary: In the hook mate a rook protected by a knight, itself anchored by a pawn, delivers checkmate to a king boxed in by its own rook.
intro: The hook mate is a checkmating pattern in which a rook, a knight and a pawn work together as a single interlocking unit. The rook delivers check right beside the enemy king, the knight protects the rook, and a pawn anchors the knight. In the diagram White plays 1.Rh7#, mating the Black king on h8. The king cannot capture the rook, cannot step to g7, and cannot retreat to g8, because its own rook stands on that square. The interlocking rook-and-knight shape gives the pattern its name.
boardCaption: White to move plays 1.Rh7#, sliding the rook from e7 to h7 along the seventh rank, where the f6-knight protects it and the Black king, hemmed in by its own rook on g8, is mated.

sections.heading: The Mating Position
paragraphs: In the diagram the Black king sits on h8 with its own rook on g8 beside it. White has a rook on e7, a knight on f6, a pawn on g5, and a king safely tucked away on b1. White ends the game at once with 1.Rh7#: the rook slides along the seventh rank from e7 to h7 and announces checkmate from the square directly beside the Black king.

Every defensive resource fails. The king cannot capture the rook on h7, because the knight on f6 defends that square, and the knight is itself protected by the pawn on g5, so even a desperate exchange is impossible. Nor can the king run: g8 is occupied by its own rook, and g7 is swept by the White rook along the seventh rank. Checked with no capture, no block possible at such close range, and no flight square, the king is mated.

sections.heading: Rook, Knight and Pawn
paragraphs: The pattern is built on a chain of protection. At the bottom sits the pawn on g5, guarding the knight on f6. The knight, in turn, guards h7, the square from which the rook gives check. Each piece supports the next, so the checking rook stands on a square the defender can never win. This interlocking rook-and-knight shape is what gives the hook mate its name, and it needs all three pieces, rook, knight and supporting pawn, working as a unit.

Just as important is the piece that takes no part in the attack at all: Black's own rook on g8. It stands on the king's natural escape square and seals it shut, leaving h8 a prison cell rather than a refuge. The hook mate characteristically features an enemy king boxed in by one of its own pieces in exactly this way. The attacker supplies the rook, knight and pawn; the defender's own army supplies the final bar of the cage, blocking the only luft the king had.

sections.heading: Recognizing It in Your Games
paragraphs: The hook mate does not appear out of nowhere; it grows from a familiar set of signals. Watch for an enemy king trapped on the edge of the board with one of its own pieces blocking its only luft, exactly as Black's rook on g8 does here. That cramped arrangement is half the mate already. The missing half is your attacking trio: ask whether a rook can reach a checking square beside the king, and whether a knight can guard that square.

When you spot such a knight, check its support next: in the diagram the g5-pawn quietly anchors the f6-knight, completing the chain of defenders the pattern needs. Train your eye to see rook, knight and pawn as one interlocking shape rather than three separate attackers. Once that unit locks together and the defending king stands on the edge with its own piece jammed beside it, the finishing blow, here 1.Rh7#, is often only a single move away.

keyIdeas: The hook mate is delivered by a rook, a knight and a supporting pawn working as a single unit.
The rook gives check from the square beside the enemy king and cannot be captured because the knight defends it.
The pawn anchors the knight, completing the chain of protection that makes the mate unbreakable.
The enemy king must be boxed in, with one of its own pieces blocking its escape square.
In the diagram 1.Rh7# mates because g8 is blocked by Black's own rook and g7 is covered along the seventh rank.
Look for the pattern when an enemy king is stuck on the edge and your knight can guard the checking square.
